# Paper money (`paper_money`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: needs paper; helped by woodblock_printing, banking_credit, quantity_theory_inflation
- Core idea: A paper note works as money when its holder can pass it on in payment. Redemption in coin or acceptance for taxes can establish demand. The Song state first issued Sichuan jiaozi in 1024. The recorded limit per issue was 1,256,340 strings of cash, with a prescribed reserve of 360,000 strings (about 29 %). Notes were exchanged for new ones at the end of their term. Specify who issues and accepts the notes, how the supply is controlled and how holders can recognise genuine notes. Seals, patterned printing and distinctive paper make imitation harder.
- Pitfalls:
  - Financing persistent deficits by issuing notes can destroy their purchasing power (late Song and Yuan notes, the Ming baochao by the mid-15th c., Law's notes 1720, Continental dollars, French assignats, Weimar 1923)
  - Refusing one's own notes in tax payments: this weakens demand for state notes, especially if holders also cannot redeem them
  - Mistaking money for wealth: extra notes do not themselves create goods; the price effect depends on output and demand for money
  - Simple printing: easy-to-copy notes invite forgers and destroy trust
  - Introducing it where people have never trusted credit or the ruler: the Ilkhanid notes of Tabriz (1294) made markets close and were withdrawn within about two months
- History: china: 9th c. – Tang 'flying money' remittance certificates (not currency); c. 1000 private issuers circulate jiaozi in Sichuan; the Song shi names sixteen wealthy households. The Yizhou bureau is authorised in 1023 and issues state notes in 1024; 1160s Southern Song huizi; 1260 Kublai's zhongtong chao, empire-wide paper currency; 1375 Ming baochao, inconvertible, abandoned in practice in the 15th c.; islamic: 1294 – Ilkhan Gaykhatu issues paper chao on the Chinese model at Tabriz; trade halts and the experiment ends within weeks; india: 1329–1332 – Muhammad bin Tughlaq issues brass and copper token coins at the value of silver; mass forgery forces their redemption, a cautionary case of fiat money without anti-counterfeiting; east_asia: c. 1600 – Yamada hagaki notes of Ise merchants in Japan; 1661 domain notes (hansatsu) of Fukui; europe: 1661 – Stockholms Banco (Palmstruch) issues the first European banknotes, fails from over-issue by 1664; 1694 Bank of England notes; 1716–1720 John Law's Banque Royale and its collapse; 1790s French assignats; americas: 1685 – New France issues money on playing cards; 1690 Massachusetts Bay issues bills of credit; 1775–1780 Continental dollars lose almost all value
- Read:
  - Richard von Glahn, Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700 (1996)
  - Marco Polo, The Description of the World (c. 1300), book II, on the Great Khan's paper money
  - Glyn Davies, A History of Money from Ancient Times to the Present Day (1994)
